lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.lesson_title: Resume: half the rectangle; match x with x
lessons.previous_learning: Math was deferred yesterday. September 30 showed a forgotten divide-by-two step and mixed coordinate positions. We have not yet checked these repair lessons.
lessons.course_context: Day 28 continues the reviewed Day 27 and restores the deferred math and writing lessons. Full Grade 6 expectations; clearer teaching, not unsupported acceleration.
learning_objectives: Explain a square unit and triangle halving
lessons.why_it_matters: These pictures help you check the answer instead of trusting a remembered rule.

vocabulary.definition: a chosen step of length
a square 1 unit wide and 1 unit tall
how much flat space a shape covers
the total distance around the edge
one number in a point’s address
a chosen side of a triangle
the distance straight across from the base at a square corner

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 10:30 to 11:15, 45 minutes. Stop at 11:15.
READ THE PICTURE: A 1-by-1 square is one square unit. A 6-by-4 rectangle has 4 rows of 6 squares: 6 × 4 = 24 square units. Area covers the inside; perimeter goes around the edge.
STEP 1: Find the area of the matching rectangle. STEP 2: Divide by 2 because two equal triangles fill that rectangle. STEP 3: Write square units. For the model, 24 ÷ 2 = 12 square units.
A right triangle has a square corner. Its base and height meet there. Do not use the sloping side as the height.
A point (x, y) is an address. The first number tells left or right; the second tells up or down. For width, compare x with x. For height, compare y with y. Do not mix their jobs.
MODEL ADDRESS: A(2,1), B(8,1), C(8,5), D(2,5). Width: 8 − 2 = 6 units. Height: 5 − 1 = 4 units. Area: 6 × 4 = 24 square units.
Try one practice item after each model. If you need help, point to the step that is confusing. At 11:15, star unfinished work and move on.

worked_examples.title: Half means divide by two
worked_examples.problem: A right triangle has base 6 units and height 4 units.
worked_examples.explanation: Two copies cover the whole rectangle; one copy covers half.

worked_examples.title: Use matching address numbers
worked_examples.explanation: First numbers give width. Second numbers give height.

independent_practice.prompt: M1. Draw one square unit and label both side lengths. Say how area differs from perimeter.
independent_practice.answer: A 1-by-1 square; area covers the inside and perimeter measures the edge.

independent_practice.prompt: M2. A right triangle has base 7 units and height 4 units. Sketch its matching rectangle. Show the rectangle area, the divide-by-two step, and the triangle area.
independent_practice.answer: 7 × 4 = 28; 28 ÷ 2 = 14 square units.

independent_practice.prompt: M3. Plot A(3,2), B(9,2), C(9,6), D(3,6) on the supplied grid. Show the x comparison, y comparison, width, height, and area.
independent_practice.answer: Width 9−3=6 units; height 6−2=4 units; area 24 square units.

independent_practice.prompt: M4. A student says a right triangle with base 5 and height 8 has area 40 square units. Explain the missed step and correct the area.
independent_practice.answer: 40 is the rectangle area; divide by2 to get 20 square units.

exit_ticket.prompt: ME1. Without the model, find the area of a right triangle with base 9 units and height 4 units. Show both steps.
ME2. Rectangle corners are (2,3), (7,3), (7,5), (2,5). Find width, height, and area. Label what each pair of numbers measures.
exit_ticket.answer: Width 5 units; height 2 units; area 10 square units.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.lesson_title: Build a clear paragraph, one sentence at a time
lessons.previous_learning: Writing was deferred yesterday. Your closeout asks for simpler help. We will keep the Grade 6 task, but build it in small steps instead of giving you a long instruction.
lessons.course_context: Day 28 continues the reviewed Day 27 and restores the deferred math and writing lessons. Full Grade 6 expectations; clearer teaching, not unsupported acceleration.
learning_objectives: Pair exact evidence with an explanation
Make and show a useful revision
lessons.why_it_matters: Readers need your explanation, not just a list of facts.

vocabulary.definition: the main idea you want to support
an exact fact from a source
why that fact supports or weakens an idea
gives a reason for an idea; does not prove it beyond doubt
change words to make your meaning clearer
a careful ending that sums up your idea

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 11:25 to 12:15, 50 minutes. Stop at 12:15.
FIRST, SAY IT: A claim is your idea. Evidence is the exact result. Reasoning explains why the result matters. Say a reason aloud before you write it.
READ THE LAMP MODEL: Bulb A stays dark. Bulb B lights in the same lamp. The lamp stays the same; the bulb changes. That is why the changed result supports a bulb problem.
USE ONE SHORT FRAME: This supports ___ because ___. Put an idea in the first gap and a real explanation in the second. “Because it is evidence” does not explain the result.
YOUR ROBOT SOURCE: The robot stops after 8 minutes with Battery A. Maya thinks the motor may be overheating. After it stops, the measured motor temperature is within the normal range. Battery A voltage drops sharply during the failure. With Battery B, the robot runs for 30 minutes without stopping. With Battery A put back, it stops again after 9 minutes.
BUILD SIX SENTENCE CARDS: 1 My claim is ___. 2 One test showed ___. 3 This supports or weakens ___ because ___. 4 Another test showed ___. 5 This supports or weakens ___ because ___. 6 Together, these tests suggest ___, although ___.
Use exact numbers when the source gives them. Join your cards into a 6-8 sentence paragraph. Read it aloud. Change one unclear sentence and show the old and new versions. You can work one card at a time.

worked_examples.title: A fact and its reason
worked_examples.problem: The same lamp stays dark with Bulb A and lights with Bulb B.
worked_examples.solution: Fact: it lights with B. Reason: this supports a bulb problem because the result changes when only the bulb changes.
worked_examples.explanation: The reason says what the result tells us, not just that a test happened.

worked_examples.title: Make the reason clearer
worked_examples.problem: Before: The test is good evidence because it is a test. After: The same lamp works with B, so A may be the problem.
worked_examples.solution: The new sentence explains the change in result and connects it to the bulb idea.
worked_examples.explanation: A revision improves meaning; checking a box is not a visible revision.

independent_practice.prompt: W1. Read the robot source. Say your claim aloud, then write it in one sentence.
independent_practice.answer: A careful claim identifies Battery A as the better-supported cause; do not require certainty.

independent_practice.prompt: W2. Choose two useful test results from the source. Write each exact fact beside a sentence explaining what it means.
independent_practice.answer: Two accurate diagnostic results, each paired with a cause-comparison reason. Accept normal temperature, voltage drop, B30-minute run, or A9-minute repeat when properly explained.

independent_practice.prompt: W3. Use the six sentence cards to write a 6-8 sentence paragraph. Use two exact results and a reason after each.
independent_practice.answer: Rubric 20: claim 4, exact relevant evidence 4, reasoning 6, organization 3, revision 3.

independent_practice.prompt: W4. Copy one unclear sentence. Write a clearer version below it. Say what you improved.
independent_practice.answer: A visible before/after change that improves meaning or structure.

exit_ticket.prompt: WE1. Underline two exact facts in your paragraph. Circle each sentence that tells why the fact matters. Explain one circled sentence aloud.
exit_ticket.answer: Two fact-reason pairs, with a meaningful explanation.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.lesson_title: Keep the match; say it aloud
lessons.previous_learning: All six written answers on Day 27 were correct. The oral cue sentences are written down accurately, but the parent speaking check is not confirmed.
lessons.course_context: Day 28 continues the reviewed Day 27 and restores the deferred math and writing lessons. Full Grade 6 expectations; clearer teaching, not unsupported acceleration.
learning_objectives: Demonstrate the three oral cues with an observer
lessons.why_it_matters: Getting the small middle word right makes the whole sentence work.

vocabulary.definition: who is doing the action
the French verb used for going to
the basic action word that stays unchanged
a sentence that says not

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 12:15 to 12:30, 15 minutes. Stop at 12:30.
KEEP THE THREE PARTS: who + matching aller + basic action word. Je vais, tu vas, il/elle va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont.
A question can start with Est-ce que. The subject still keeps its matching verb. Tu goes with vas, even inside a question.
For not, put ne and pas around the aller form. Before a vowel, ne becomes n’. Example: Nous n’allons pas dessiner.
Today’s actions: parler = speak; chanter = sing; écouter = listen. Spend about 5 minutes on the model and writing, then 5 minutes on the parent-observed oral check. Use the remaining time for one retry.

worked_examples.title: Ask a question
worked_examples.explanation: Tu keeps vas; dessiner stays unchanged.

worked_examples.title: Say not
worked_examples.problem: She is not going to draw.
worked_examples.explanation: Ne and pas go around va.

independent_practice.prompt: F1. Translate: You are going to speak. Use tu.
independent_practice.answer: Tu vas parler.

independent_practice.prompt: F2. Turn Tu vas chanter into an Est-ce que question.
independent_practice.answer: Est-ce que tu vas chanter ?

independent_practice.prompt: F3. Make negative: Nous allons écouter.
independent_practice.answer: Nous n’allons pas écouter.

exit_ticket.prompt: FE1. Without the chart, SAY: You are going to watch (tu); Are you going to read (tu); We are not going to play. Parent records correct/retry for each spoken first try and after retry.
exit_ticket.answer: Tu vas regarder. Est-ce que tu vas lire ? Nous n’allons pas jouer. Written forms alone do not confirm speaking.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.lesson_title: The mirror must match the turn
lessons.previous_learning: Your Day 27 path now changes direction twice. But Mirror 2 tilts up-right while the ray leaves left. Fix the mirror direction, not just the arrow. Your science picture was the most helpful part.
lessons.course_context: Day 28 continues the reviewed Day 27 and restores the deferred math and writing lessons. Full Grade 6 expectations; clearer teaching, not unsupported acceleration.
learning_objectives: Match mirror tilt to the ray direction
Draw a perpendicular normal at each hit
Explain why the normal turns with its mirror
lessons.why_it_matters: A clear drawing lets you test whether light could really reach the target.

vocabulary.definition: a surface that bounces light
a line showing which way light travels
a helper line making a square corner with the mirror
meeting at a square corner
moving toward the mirror
moving away from the mirror
bounce off a surface

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 1:00 to 1:30, 30 minutes. Stop at 1:30.
LOOK AT THE TWO PICTURES: An upward ray hitting an up-right mirror turns right. To turn that upward ray left, use a down-right mirror. Changing the arrow alone does not change what the mirror can do.
DRAW IN THIS ORDER: 1 Mirror. 2 Hit point. 3 Dashed normal at a square corner. 4 Incoming arrow. 5 Outgoing arrow with the same angle on the other side of the normal.
The normal belongs to its mirror. When a mirror turns, its normal turns too. That changes the reflected path, so the ray may miss the next mirror.
At EACH mirror, check the square corner, the incoming/outgoing arrows, and equal angle marks from the normal. Equal numbers do not repair a wrong direction. Use a ruler and protractor if available; do not claim exact measurements from a rough sketch.

worked_examples.title: One bounce
worked_examples.problem: Light hits a horizontal mirror at 45 degrees from the vertical normal.
worked_examples.solution: It leaves at 45 degrees on the other side of that normal.
worked_examples.explanation: Both angles are measured from the dashed line, not from the mirror.

worked_examples.title: Make the top ray go left
worked_examples.problem: Light travels right, then up. The target is to the left of the top hit point.
worked_examples.solution: Use an up-right first mirror and a down-right second mirror. Draw a new perpendicular normal at each hit point.
worked_examples.explanation: The second mirror orientation must agree with the outgoing direction.

independent_practice.prompt: S1. Correct your Day 27 two-mirror drawing. Keep the leftward target. Redraw Mirror 2 and its normal; add right-angle squares, both hit points, and equal-angle marks. Keep the original visible.
independent_practice.answer: Mirror 1 up-right; Mirror 2 down-right; normals perpendicular; right/up/left arrows; matching angles at each hit.

independent_practice.prompt: S2. Draw a NEW route starting at the bottom: ray goes up, then right, then up to a target. Choose two mirrors that make those turns. Label both normals and angle marks.
independent_practice.answer: Both mirrors up-right; both normals down-right; two consistent 90-degree turns with 45-degree angles from each normal.

exit_ticket.prompt: SE1. If Mirror 1 turns, what happens to its normal, and why might the ray miss Mirror 2?
exit_ticket.answer: Normal turns with mirror; outgoing path changes, potentially missing Mirror 2.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.lesson_title: Replace “good choices” with a real action
lessons.previous_learning: You correctly explained that boats and trading places matter. Your two-sentence explanation still says people made choices without naming a place and a specific action.
lessons.course_context: Day 28 continues the reviewed Day 27 and restores the deferred math and writing lessons. Full Grade 6 expectations; clearer teaching, not unsupported acceleration.
learning_objectives: Explain how a feature creates an opportunity, not a guarantee
lessons.why_it_matters: History gets clearer when you explain how people used a place.

vocabulary.definition: a part of a place, such as a river or hill
something people actually do
what can happen because of the action
something helpful, not a promise of success

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 1:30 to 1:55, 25 minutes. Stop at 1:55.
USE THREE BOXES: PLACE → PEOPLE DO SOMETHING → POSSIBLE RESULT. Do not stop at “people make good choices.” Name the action so a reader can picture it.
Rome had the Tiber River, nearby farmland, and hills. A river can provide a route, but people must use boats to carry goods. Farmland can support crops, but farmers must plant and harvest them.
MODEL: A useful road → people carry goods along it → buyers can receive the goods. The road is helpful, but the action explains how people use it.
Today we make the explanation specific before the Republic. Use your existing history video observation as context; you do not need to watch it again. Do not test later Roman rulers today.

worked_examples.title: A road needs users
worked_examples.problem: A town is beside a road.
worked_examples.solution: People carry goods on the road, so goods can reach buyers.
worked_examples.explanation: Names the feature, an observable action, and a possible result.

worked_examples.title: Replace a vague phrase
worked_examples.problem: Before: People made good choices. After: People used boats to carry goods on the river.
worked_examples.solution: The new version tells the reader exactly what people did.
worked_examples.explanation: Good is an opinion; the boat action is something we can describe.

independent_practice.prompt: H1. Complete three boxes for the Tiber River: feature; a specific human action; a possible result.
independent_practice.answer: River; people use boats to transport goods; goods reach buyers/trade becomes easier.

independent_practice.prompt: H2. Repair your Day 27 H3 answer in two sentences. Name one Roman geographic feature and say exactly how people used it.
independent_practice.answer: Specific river/farmland/hills example and action, plus geography-helped-not-alone explanation.

exit_ticket.prompt: HE1. A town has fertile farmland, but nobody plants crops. Does the land alone feed the town? Explain the missing action.
exit_ticket.answer: No; farmers must plant, tend, and harvest crops. Helpful geography is not enough by itself.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.previous_learning: You have built apps and games before. Today explore a new creative setting: sci-fi, a mysterious museum, fantasy, or your own idea. The unfinished ScoutLab rating checks do not block this build.
lessons.course_context: Day 28 Builder replacement requested by parent: ambitious, enjoyable project work using AI-assisted coding and practical integrations. Keep testing inside real game play. Preserve all other subjects and past grades.
learning_objectives: Direct an AI coding tool to create a playable game
Connect one chosen feature to an existing working game
Use playtesting to improve a visible bug or design problem
lessons.why_it_matters: You can invent a world, give its characters rules, and turn your idea into something another person can explore.

vocabulary.definition: a first version you can try
the repeated cycle: move, react, draw the next moment
rules that make an opponent react to you
connecting one tool or feature to another
play on purpose to find what feels good or breaks
find why something went wrong and fix it

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 40 minutes total. This replaces only today's Computer Science/Builder block. Use elapsed time if you start late; do not extend the whole school day.
LAPTOP ONLY. Today you are the game director: choose the look, ask the AI to build, and judge the game by playing it. Save ScoutLab as it is. Its unfinished rating checks are not a gate for this new build.
MINUTES 0-4: Choose Portal Escape, Museum After Dark, or Dragon Rescue. Open your usual AI coding workspace with a runnable preview. Name your project. Replace the bracketed world choice in the build prompt with your choice. You can invent your own setting using the same find-item, evade-guard, reach-exit mission.
MINUTES 4-22: Paste the build prompt below. Run the result immediately. Move, collect the special item, evade the guard, and reach the exit. If the first version fails, send the exact error or describe what you see. Use the remaining build time to make the core playable.
BUILD PROMPT: Build a playable browser adventure called World Builder. I am the creative director. Give me a working preview and editable project, not just a plan. My chosen world is [PORTAL ESCAPE / MUSEUM AFTER DARK / DRAGON RESCUE]. Use my chosen setting for the characters, colors, objects, and ending. Make one small 3D scene using Three.js if this workspace supports it. If 3D cannot run here, tell me and make a polished top-down Canvas version with the same play. Use simple shapes first so the game can run quickly. Use an angled camera that keeps the whole area and the player visible. Controls: WASD or arrow keys to move; E to interact when near an object. Show the controls and the current goal on screen. Keep the player inside the world. Add Start, Pause, and Restart. The mission: find one special item, get past one moving guard, and reach the exit. Portal Escape uses an energy core, a robot sentry, and a portal. Museum After Dark uses a moon key, a living statue, and a moonlit door. Dragon Rescue uses a healing crystal, a stone golem, and a dragon nest. Show a clear ending when I arrive at the exit with the item. The guard patrols between two places. When I come close, it chases my current position at a beatable speed. If I move far away, it returns to patrol. It cannot teleport or know my next key press. If it catches me, return me to the start and reset the item. This is a rule-based character, not a trained machine-learning model. An exit stays closed until I collect the item with E. Show a nearby interaction hint, then show the collected item in a small on-screen bag. The item disappears from the world when collected. Pause freezes movement. Restart resets the player, guard, item, exit, and messages. Holding E must not trigger repeated wins. Use smooth movement, dramatic lighting or color, clear silhouettes, and a short exit celebration. No quizzes, arithmetic gates, accounts, paid services, or multiplayer today. Ask at most one essential question, then build the playable version. Explain one important game rule in plain language after it runs.
MINUTES 22-32: Once the mission works, choose ONE upgrade: responsive sound, your own world art, or a talking character. Paste its prompt. If the core is still broken, use this time to repair it. A playable smaller game is a successful first version.
SOUND THAT RESPONDS: Add original browser-generated sound for collecting the item, being spotted, and opening the exit. Start audio after I press Start. Add Mute. Keep movement and interactions working.
MY WORLD ART: Use an image-generation tool available to me to make an original backdrop for my chosen world, without words. I will attach the image to the coding chat. Add it behind the play area or as a scene object; keep the player and exits visible. If image generation is unavailable, create an original backdrop in code.
A TALKING CHARACTER: Add a friendly character near the start. When I press E nearby, show one short hint in a speech bubble. Add a Speak button using browser text-to-speech when supported. Keep the text visible if speech is unavailable. The hint should fit my world and help me discover what to do.
MINUTES 32-38: Play your mission. Try the exit before and after collecting the item. Get spotted, then try escaping the guard. Try Pause and Restart. Pick the most annoying bug or design problem and improve it. DEBUG PROMPT: When I [action], I expected [what should happen], but [what I saw]. Here is a screenshot or exact error if available. Find the cause, fix this feature, and keep the working movement and interactions. Then tell me which part changed in plain language.
MINUTES 38-40: Save the project or export its files using your workspace. Show one live round or save a short screen recording. Say what you chose, what improved, and what you would add next. No paper test log. If unfinished, save the working version or current error and pick up there next time.

worked_examples.title: Direct a character with a clear rule
worked_examples.problem: Make the guard smarter is too vague. What should a player see?
worked_examples.solution: Say: Walk between the two pillars. When I come close, chase me. When I escape far enough, return to the pillars.
worked_examples.explanation: Patrol, chase, and return are three clear behaviors. This is game AI made from rules.

worked_examples.title: Fix a real game problem
worked_examples.problem: In an example racing game, Restart moves the car back but leaves the old timer running.
worked_examples.solution: Tell the AI: Restart returns my car to the start, but the timer still shows the old time. Reset the timer as well. Keep steering working. Then restart twice and drive again.
worked_examples.explanation: Name the action and the visible problem. After the fix, try the same action and a control that worked before.

independent_practice.prompt: B1. Choose a world. Build and run the adventure using the ready-to-paste prompt. Move, collect the item, evade the guard, and reach the exit.
independent_practice.answer: A playable small adventure, or a saved partial build with a clearly described blocker. The student chooses a setting and demonstrates working interactions. Use the top-down fallback if 3D cannot run.

independent_practice.prompt: B2. Once the mission works, add one upgrade: responsive sound, your own world art, or a talking character. Otherwise repair the core.
independent_practice.answer: A connected, visible or audible feature that works with the existing game. Repairing a broken core also earns credit for iteration; do not require all three upgrades.

independent_practice.prompt: B3. Play, find one real bug or design problem, and ask for a focused improvement. Save the playable version or your current blocker.
independent_practice.answer: Demonstrate the before/after behavior where possible. If no technical bug appears, improve fairness, controls, or readability and explain the choice. No invented bug and no paper log.

exit_ticket.prompt: Show your game for one minute. What did you direct the AI to change, and did that change make the game better?
exit_ticket.answer: A brief live demonstration or recording plus the student's own explanation. Assess decisions and iteration, not typing code from memory.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: One clue card you can check
lessons.previous_learning: You logged pages 70-80 for 25 minutes. You named an explosion and Otis delivering letters, but not a page/chapter or another possible meaning. The explosion needs a clearer link before it supports an Otis theory.
lessons.course_context: Day 28 continues the reviewed Day 27 and restores the deferred math and writing lessons. Full Grade 6 expectations; clearer teaching, not unsupported acceleration.
learning_objectives: Find and locate one exact detail
Separate a clue from a theory
lessons.why_it_matters: A mystery theory becomes stronger when you can show the clue behind it.

vocabulary.definition: exact words or an action you can find in the book
the page or chapter where you found a detail
your idea about what the detail might mean
another possible explanation
an idea that can change when you find new evidence

lessons.written_instruction:
TIME CAP: 2:45 to 3:20, 35 minutes. Stop at 3:20.
START AT YOUR ACTUAL BOOKMARK, near page 80 in your edition. Spend up to 5 minutes locating ONE detail from yesterday. Write its page or chapter. If you cannot find it, replace it and say you changed your detail.
READ QUIETLY FOR 25 MINUTES. Virgil stays quiet unless you ask for a word meaning. Record starting page, ending page, and minutes. Do not force a chapter or look ahead.
MAKE ONE CLUE CARD: Exact detail + page/chapter + my idea + another possibility + keep/change and why. You do not need to write four separate long answers.
ASK: Does this detail point specifically to my character, or could it fit several people? “Still suspicious” is not a new piece of evidence. Use may or might when the idea is uncertain.
Use only the pages you have read. The Westing Game’s 8 reading points are still pending until completion and a comprehension check. No spoilers or invented book details.

worked_examples.title: A clue is not proof
worked_examples.problem: In an invented story, Mina has mud on her shoes at page 6.
worked_examples.solution: Detail: muddy shoes, page 6. Idea: she may have crossed the garden. Alternative: she may have used another muddy path.
worked_examples.explanation: The locator makes the detail checkable; the two ideas remain possible.

worked_examples.title: Change with new evidence
worked_examples.problem: Later in the invented story, Mina says she walked beside the stream.
worked_examples.solution: I change my garden idea because the new statement names a different muddy route.
worked_examples.explanation: Explain the new evidence, not merely that the character still seems suspicious.

independent_practice.prompt: L1. Record today’s actual starting page, ending page, and 25 minutes of reading.
independent_practice.answer: A genuine reading log; no invented target page.

independent_practice.prompt: L2. Complete ONE clue card with five fields: exact detail; page/chapter; your idea; another possible explanation; keep/change with a reason.
independent_practice.answer: Rubric 10: exact detail 2, locator 2, plausible idea 2, plausible alternative 2, decision with evidence link 2. Check against the student’s edition without spoilers.

exit_ticket.prompt: LE1. Point to the page/chapter behind your card. Explain whether it singles out one person or could fit more than one.
exit_ticket.answer: Student points to a real locator and explains the limits of the chosen evidence.
